title: US Reaper Drone Fleet Falls Below Safety Threshold After Billion-Dollar Losses in Iran War
excerpt: At least 24 MQ-9 Reapers were destroyed during Operation Epic Fury, costing up to $1.2 billion and leaving the Air Force scrambling for replacements after the production line was shut down.
body:
• A Congressional Research Service report confirmed 24 MQ-9 Reaper drones destroyed during Operation Epic Fury, with some estimates putting the toll closer to 30
  • Losses worth up to $1.2 billion have dropped the fleet to roughly 135 aircraft — 54 below the Air Force's 189-drone operational minimum
  • General Atomics shut down the MQ-9A production line in 2025, leaving fewer than 10 new airframes available for purchase
  • The Pentagon is now pursuing cheaper, mass-producible drone alternatives designed to absorb losses in contested airspace

The U.S. Air Force's fleet of MQ-9 Reaper drones has fallen well below its operational floor after sustaining heavy losses during the six-week air campaign against Iran, forcing a strategic reckoning over the future of America's most relied-upon unmanned combat platform.

A Congressional Research Service report confirmed that 24 MQ-9 Reapers were destroyed during Operation Epic Fury, the U.S.-Israeli air campaign that ran from February 28 through early April 2026. Other assessments, cited by Bloomberg and military analysts, put the tally closer to 30. At up to $50 million per fully equipped airframe, according to testimony by Maj. Gen. Christopher Niemi before the Senate on May 12, the hardware bill could reach $1.2 billion.

The Drone That Became the War's MVP

The scale of the losses is matched by the scale of the Reaper's contribution. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told the House Armed Services Committee on May 20 that the MQ-9 was "perhaps the most valuable player" of the entire campaign — a striking endorsement from a career fighter pilot.

https://x.com/War_Radar2/status/2088065437934473251

"No other platform is even close to the MQ-9."

— Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach, Air Force Chief of Staff

Capable of staying airborne for more than 24 hours, Reapers flew roughly a dozen orbits over Iran at peak tempo, striking mobile missile launchers and feeding targeting data to manned aircraft. More than 4,000 of the campaign's 13,000-plus targets were dynamic — mobile launchers and weapons systems requiring immediate engagement that manned fighters, with their limited loiter time, could not reliably cover.

In one instance, a Reaper engaged Iranian forces closing within three kilometers of a downed F-15E Strike Eagle crew member, providing critical force protection.

Iran's Air Defenses Exploited a Known Weakness

Iran's electro-optical and infrared surface-to-air missile systems, whose passive sensors give little radar warning, proved effective against the Reaper's large, slow-flying profile. Many drones were shot down mid-flight, while others were destroyed on the ground as Iran systematically targeted U.S. regional bases.

The Reaper fleet now stands at approximately 135 aircraft, according to Lt. Gen. David Tabor's Senate testimony — 54 below the service's long-standing 189-aircraft operational floor.

No Easy Path to Replacement

The losses have exposed a supply crisis. General Atomics shut down the MQ-9A production line in 2025 after the Air Force confirmed it would stop buying the platform. A company spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine that fewer than 10 new or company-owned MQ-9As remain available for sale. The Air Force is examining whether to pull aircraft from the Boneyard at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base.

"We are not divesting the MQ-9. We have had some losses in that aircraft, and we're working to fill those losses."

— Troy Meink, Secretary of the Air Force

The budget disconnect drew pointed criticism from lawmakers. Rep. John Garamendi (D-CA) noted the fiscal year 2027 request allocates $7.4 billion for F-35s and $5 billion for the next-generation F-47 fighter, against just $1.4 billion for Collaborative Combat Aircraft — autonomous wingmen designed to complement manned jets.

Pentagon Pivots to Cheaper, Expendable Drones

The Defense Innovation Unit has opened submissions for the Massed Modular Aircraft (MMA) program, seeking theater-range drones that are modular, mass-producible, and built around the expectation that some will be lost. Specifications call for at least 2,800 pounds of payload, a 2,300-nautical-mile combat radius, and speeds of at least 200 knots.

Separately, Maj. Gen. Niemi signed requirements on May 11 for a new "attritable" medium-altitude drone to succeed the MQ-9A, with up to 932 miles of range and at least 20 hours of endurance at a "low-to-medium acquisition cost." The Pentagon has also deployed the Low-Cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System (LUCAS) in Iran — a drone costing roughly $35,000 and modeled on Iran's Shahed designs.

What's Next

The Air Force's $996.5 million request for initial Collaborative Combat Aircraft production in fiscal 2027, plus roughly $1.37 billion in research and development, marks the first time the program has reached formal production funding. The service aims to field more than 150 CCAs before the end of the Future Years Defense Program.

But the immediate challenge remains filling the Reaper gap. The campaign proved that persistent, sensor-rich unmanned platforms are indispensable in modern air combat — and that the economics of losing $30-to-$50-million drones against adversaries with cheap anti-aircraft systems are unsustainable.
